analysis.one_liner: Guarantees all Americans affordable, standardized health coverage, financed by new taxes on tobacco, premiums, and high-cost plans.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee's compromise health reform bill was reported on August 2, 1994 and debated on the Senate floor for nearly two weeks, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended January 3, 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the Senate Finance Committee's rewritten version of the 1994 health reform effort: it would have required every state to certify health plans that cannot turn people away for preexisting conditions or charge sick customers more, created purchasing cooperatives so individuals and small employers can buy coverage at group rates, and provided premium subsidies for low-income people. It would have paid for this with higher tobacco and ammunition taxes, a tax on high-cost insurance plans, a tax on health insurance premiums and self-insured plans, recapture of subsidies from high earners, and cuts to some Medicare payments. States could have chosen to run their own single-payer systems instead. The Senate debated the bill in August 1994 but never brought it to a vote, and the session ended without action.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly millions of Americans who in 1994 had no insurance or could be denied or priced out of coverage: the bill required guaranteed issue and renewal, barred charging people more for being sick, set a standard benefits package, and gave low-income people premium and cost-sharing help through Medicaid. Small-business workers would gain access to purchasing cooperatives, and rural areas would get new grants, telemedicine projects, and community health groups.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people denied coverage

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated purpose is to achieve universal health insurance coverage through subsidies, affordable standardized insurance, and an end to insurance companies' exclusionary practices.
It requires states to certify health plans meeting standards including guaranteed issue and renewal, community rating, and nondiscrimination based on health status.

It creates a Medicaid-based program of premium and cost-sharing assistance for low-income individuals, plus grants for community health groups, rural telemedicine, and expanded coverage of nurse practitioners and home and community-based care for disabled and frail elderly people.
It would have repealed the health insurance industry's antitrust immunity under the McCarran-Ferguson Act and set new disclosure and qualification rules for nonprofit health care organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco users through higher excise taxes; health plans and self-insured employers through new assessments and a 25% tax on high-cost plans; high-income individuals through recapture of health subsidies and taxation of flexible spending accounts; S corporation shareholders and limited partners through self-employment tax changes; state and local government employees newly covered by the Medicare tax; and hospitals, teaching programs, and other providers through Medicare payment cuts, a freeze on skilled nursing facility updates, and termination of indirect medical education payments. Malpractice claimants would face mandatory alternative dispute resolution before suing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco users, insurers, high earners, providers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself guarantee universal coverage: if fewer than 95 percent of residents are covered by 2002, a National Health Commission would submit an implementing bill to Congress, so full coverage depends on future action.

Part of the financing falls directly on ordinary people: higher cigarette and tobacco taxes, a new tax on roll-your-own tobacco, higher taxes on hollow-point and large-caliber handgun ammunition, and taxation of health benefits previously provided tax-free through flexible spending accounts.

Large employers with 100 or more full-time workers may keep their own experience-rated self-insured plans outside the community-rated market, creating a two-tier system in which employees of small firms buy through purchasing cooperatives while employees of big employers stay in a separate pool.

Federal malpractice rules would require claims to go through state alternative dispute resolution procedures before any lawsuit could be brought in participating states, limiting injured patients' access to court, and the bill preempts some state insurance and benefit-mandate laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — guaranteed, community-rated coverage for everyone, with subsidies for those who cannot afford it — was the largest proposed expansion of health security in generations, and its costs to ordinary people (mainly tobacco taxes and some Medicare cuts) are real but modest compared with the gain of universal coverage. Its genuine design flaws are that full universal coverage is deferred to a future commission, large employers are carved out of the community-rated pool, and malpractice claimants lose direct access to courts. On balance this was a broadly helpful bill whose main costs fell on insurers, tobacco users, high earners, and some providers.

outcome.mechanism: The Finance Committee reported the bill and put it on the Senate calendar in August 1994, the Senate debated it for about two weeks that month, but no vote was ever taken and the Congress ended January 3, 1995, killing the bill.

narrative.text: The Senate Finance Committee ordered an original bill reported on July 2, 1994, and Senator Moynihan reported it to the Senate with written report 103-323 on August 2, 1994.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 539 and was laid before the Senate by unanimous consent on August 9, 1994.
The Senate considered the bill in floor debate from August 9 through August 19, 1994, but the record shows no vote on passage, no cloture vote, and no further action after August 19.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill received no further action, so it died without ever coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, large self-insured employers, tobacco manufacturers, and the provider groups that opposed the payment cuts and malpractice changes kept the status quo. Millions of uninsured Americans remained without the guaranteed coverage the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, big employers, and tobacco makers

for.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
for.role: Chair, Senate Finance Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and reported it to the Senate from the Finance Committee as an original measure on August 2, 1994.

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the original bill reported on July 2, 1994, producing this rewritten, compromise version of the Health Security Act.

for.name: Senate Democratic leadership
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor by unanimous consent on August 9, 1994 and led roughly two weeks of floor debate, but never brought it to a final vote before the session ended.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Made universal health coverage the top domestic priority of 1994 and pushed Congress to pass health reform, of which this Finance Committee bill was one of the competing versions.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and were prepared to use extended debate and procedural delay to keep it from an up-or-down vote, preventing the 60 votes needed to end debate.

against.name: Health insurance industry, led by the Health Insurance Association of America
against.what_they_did: Ran a public campaign against the reform, including the widely seen 'Harry and Louise' advertising, urging viewers to contact Congress in opposition.

against.name: Small-business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied heavily against the bill's employer coverage requirements and new taxes on health benefits and self-insured plans.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote was ever taken, so the record contains no vote breakdown; in the 56-to-43 Democratic-majority Senate, floor support came from Democrats while Republicans opposed the bill and blocked it from a final vote.

industries.note: The bill would have made private health plans the permanent channel for nearly all Americans' coverage, guaranteeing them tens of millions of new customers, while stripping their antitrust immunity and forcing community rating, guaranteed issue, new assessments, and a 25% tax on high-cost plans. The industry opposed the bill despite being locked into its role, because the rating and tax rules cut into profits from cherry-picking healthy customers.

Employers with 100 or more full-time workers could keep their own experience-rated self-insured plans outside the community-rated pool, but faced new enrollment duties, reserve requirements for post-retirement benefits, and federal oversight of multistate plans.
The bill raises excise taxes on cigarettes, other tobacco products, and roll-your-own tobacco, partly to fund subsidies for children and pregnant women; the cost passes to consumers as higher prices.

They would lose through Medicare payment cuts, reduced disproportionate share payments, a freeze on skilled nursing facility updates, and termination of indirect medical education payments, but gain a new Graduate Medical Education and Academic Health Centers Trust Fund and payments to hospitals serving vulnerable populations.

Mandatory alternative dispute resolution before any lawsuit, plus federal tort rules preempting state law, would sharply reduce malpractice litigation, lowering insurers' exposure and limiting injured patients' day in court.
